nameStory: Atlantic Sturgeon gets its name from being found along the Atlantic coast, while 'sturgeon' comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'to stir up' - referring to how these massive fish churn up mud and sediment when feeding on the bottom. These living fossils have been stirring up Atlantic waters for over 120 million years!
description: Atlantic Sturgeon are truly impressive prehistoric fish that can grow enormous - some reaching over 14 feet long and weighing hundreds of pounds. Their most striking feature is their armor-like appearance, with five rows of bony plates called scutes running along their diamond-shaped body instead of regular scales. They have a shark-like tail, a long pointed snout, and four whisker-like barbels hanging from their underside that help them find food. These ancient giants are olive-green to bluish-black on top with a pale belly.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Unmistakable diamond-shaped, torpedo body with five distinct rows of hard, bony plates (scutes) that feel like armor when touched - no other New England fish has this prehistoric appearance

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Tube-like, toothless mouth positioned underneath the head, perfect for vacuum-feeding on the bottom; feels soft and rubbery if you can get close enough

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Distinctive shark-like tail with upper lobe longer than lower, plus a long-based dorsal fin positioned far back on the body

idTips.label: Sensory Features
idTips.description: Four barbels (whisker-like organs) hang from the underside like a mustache, used to taste and feel for food in muddy bottoms

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark olive-green to bluish-black back fading to pale yellow or white belly; young fish may have more distinct banding

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Massive fish - adults commonly 6-8 feet, but can exceed 14 feet and 800 pounds; even juveniles are surprisingly hefty compared to other local fish

habitat: Atlantic Sturgeon spend most of their adult lives in coastal ocean waters but return to New England's major rivers like the Connecticut, Merrimack, and Kennebec to spawn. Look for them in deep river channels with strong currents and rocky or sandy bottoms during spring and early summer. They prefer areas where fresh and salt water mix, often near river mouths and estuaries.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot them as adults migrate up major rivers to spawn, often visible near river mouths and in deeper pools of large rivers like the Connecticut.
seasonality.summer: Spawning activity continues in early summer; young fish may be found in river nursery areas with muddy bottoms rich in invertebrates.
seasonality.fall: Adults begin moving back toward ocean waters; juveniles remain in rivers feeding heavily to build energy for winter.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed as they move to deeper ocean waters or deeper river pools; metabolism slows significantly in cold water.

funFact: Atlantic Sturgeon can live over 60 years and don't even start reproducing until they're 10-30 years old - imagine a fish that's older than most people before it has its first babies! Some of the largest individuals swimming in New England waters today may have been born when your grandparents were children.
confusionNotes: In New England waters, Atlantic Sturgeon are virtually unmistakable due to their massive size and armored appearance - no other fish comes close to looking like these living dinosaurs. The bony scutes and barbels make identification foolproof even at a distance.
contextualKnowledge: Atlantic Sturgeon are protected under the Endangered Species Act, so any sightings should be reported to wildlife authorities and the fish should never be harmed or harassed. These ancient fish were nearly wiped out by overfishing for their valuable eggs (caviar) and meat in the 1800s and early 1900s.
compareHints: As the only sturgeon species regularly found in New England waters, Atlantic Sturgeon stands alone in its distinctive appearance. While other sturgeon species exist in North America, none occur in our region, making identification straightforward - if you see a large fish with bony plates and barbels in New England, it's an Atlantic Sturgeon.
